title: Effects of Structured Aerobic Exercise on Sleep Quality in Sedentary Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: Background: Sedentary lifestyle is associated with poor sleep quality. Methods: A randomized controlled trial was conducted with 120 sedentary adults aged 50-70 years. Participants were assigned to either a 12-week aerobic exercise program (n=60) or standard care control group (n=60). The exercise group completed 45 minutes of moderate-intensity walking 3 times per week. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline and 12 weeks. Results: The exercise group showed significant improvement in PSQI scores (mean change: -3.2) compared to control (mean change: -0.5, p<0.001). Improved sleep efficiency was maintained at 24-week follow-up. Conclusion: Structured aerobic exercise significantly improves sleep quality in sedentary middle-aged adults.

title: Cross-Sectional Analysis of Exercise Duration and Sleep Efficiency in Shift Workers
abstract: Objective: To examine the relationship between exercise duration and sleep quality metrics in shift workers. Design: This cross-sectional analysis enrolled 200 shift workers from three urban hospitals. Sleep efficiency was measured using wrist actigraphy over 7 days. Exercise duration was self-reported. Data analysis: Linear regression models controlled for age, sex, and work shift type. Results: Each additional 30 minutes of weekly exercise was associated with a 2.1% improvement in sleep efficiency (95% CI: 0.8-3.4%, p=0.002). This association remained significant after adjustment for confounders. Conclusion: Regular exercise is associated with improved sleep efficiency in shift workers, suggesting a potential intervention target.

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Exercise Interventions for Sleep Disorders
abstract: Background: Multiple randomized trials have examined exercise for sleep improvement, but results are inconsistent. Methods: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane databases through December 2023 for randomized controlled trials examining exercise and sleep outcomes in adults. Included studies: 45 randomized trials were identified and screened. 28 trials met inclusion criteria (total participants across studies: 3,847). Primary analysis: Meta-analysis using random-effects models assessed change in sleep quality (PSQI scores). Results: Exercise interventions showed moderate improvement in PSQI scores (standardized mean difference: -0.52, 95% CI: -0.72 to -0.31). Subgroup analysis by exercise type (aerobic vs. resistance) showed similar benefits. Heterogeneity: I-squared = 68%, indicating moderate heterogeneity. Conclusion: Exercise is an effective intervention for improving sleep quality in adults. Future research should examine optimal exercise dose and timing.

title: A 16-Week Yoga-Based Intervention for Sleep Quality and Anxiety in Healthcare Workers
abstract: Background: Healthcare workers report high rates of sleep disturbance and anxiety. Methods: All enrolled healthcare workers (n=85) from two urban hospitals completed baseline assessments. The intervention group (45 workers) attended twice-weekly 60-minute yoga sessions for 16 weeks; the control group (40 workers) received sleep hygiene education only. Sleep quality was measured using PSQI; anxiety using the GAD-7 scale. Results: Of the 85 enrolled, 73 completed the intervention (8 yoga, 4 control dropped out). Among completers, yoga improved PSQI scores by 5.2 points versus 1.1 points in control (p=0.008). Anxiety also improved significantly in the yoga group. Limitations: Non-randomized, single-site design. Conclusion: Yoga may improve sleep and anxiety in healthcare workers, warranting larger randomized trials.

title: Protocol for a Cluster-Randomized Trial of Community-Based Exercise Programs on Sleep and Cardiovascular Health
abstract: Background: Community-based exercise programs are scalable interventions, but evidence is limited. Study Design: This protocol describes a cluster-randomized trial of 16 community centers in three regions, randomizing at the center level (8 intervention, 8 control). Planned Sample Size: We aim to recruit 400 adults aged 40-70 years (approximately 25 per center). Intervention: Exercise instructors will deliver 90-minute mixed-modal exercise sessions (aerobic, resistance, flexibility) twice weekly for 12 months. Primary Outcomes: Sleep efficiency (actigraphy) and resting heart rate. Secondary Outcomes: PSQI scores, blood pressure. Data Collection: Baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. Statistical Analysis: Intention-to-treat analysis accounting for cluster randomization using generalized estimating equations. Timeline: Recruitment began January 2024; follow-up expected to conclude December 2025. Ethical Approval: Approved by [Institution] IRB [number]. Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov [identifier pending]. Conclusion: This protocol will provide evidence for scalable community-based exercise interventions.

title: Qualitative Study of Exercise Experiences and Sleep Improvement in Middle-Aged Women
abstract: Objective: To explore how middle-aged women experience exercise and perceive its effects on sleep. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 25 women aged 45-60 who had increased exercise participation in the prior year. Participants were recruited through community centers and online forums. Analysis: Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Themes: Participants described improved sleep quality, increased energy, and enhanced mood. Many noted that exercise timing mattered (morning vs. evening). Barriers: Time constraints, initial fatigue, and self-doubt were mentioned. Facilitators: Social support, enjoyable activities, and perceived health benefits sustained engagement. Conclusion: Women perceived meaningful sleep and health benefits from exercise, but personalization of timing and activity type is important for sustained participation.

title: Effect of High-Intensity Interval Training on Sleep Architecture and Cardiovascular Outcomes
abstract: Background: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is time-efficient, but effects on sleep remain unclear. Methods: This 8-week pilot study included 40 previously sedentary adults. Participants underwent polysomnography (PSG) at baseline and post-intervention. Exercise protocol: The intervention group (n=20) completed three 20-minute HIIT sessions weekly; control (n=20) maintained baseline activity. PSG measured sleep duration, slow-wave sleep percentage, and REM sleep. Cardiovascular: VO2 max and resting heart rate were measured. Results: Of 40 enrolled, 32 completed post-intervention assessments (6 intervention, 2 control lost to follow-up). The HIIT group showed increased slow-wave sleep (baseline: 18%, post: 23%, p=0.04) and slightly reduced sleep latency. VO2 max improved by 12% in the HIIT group. Conclusion: HIIT may increase slow-wave sleep, supporting cognitive and metabolic recovery. Larger studies are needed to confirm findings.

title: Sleep and Exercise Patterns in Shift Workers: A Cohort Study
abstract: Study Design: This prospective cohort study followed shift workers over 12 months to examine associations between exercise patterns and sleep outcomes. Recruitment: Participants were recruited from three manufacturing facilities. Sleep and exercise were measured using wrist actigraphy and self-report. Exposure: Exercise was categorized as low (<30 min/week), moderate (30-150 min/week), or high (>150 min/week). Outcome: Sleep efficiency measured via actigraphy. Analysis: Adjusted linear regression controlled for age, shift type, and caffeine use. Results: Compared to low exercise, moderate and high exercise were associated with 8.2% and 11.5% improvements in sleep efficiency, respectively. These associations were stronger in night-shift workers. Conclusion: Exercise may partially mitigate the adverse effects of shift work on sleep, particularly for night-shift workers.

title: Running and Sleep Quality: Evidence from the National Health Survey
abstract: Methods: Data from 15,000 adults in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) were analyzed. Sleep quality was assessed using a standardized questionnaire. Running participation was self-reported. Analysis: Logistic regression assessed the association between running and good sleep quality, adjusted for age, BMI, income, and health conditions. Results: Adults who reported regular running (≥3 days/week) had 23% lower odds of poor sleep quality (OR: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.65-0.91) compared to sedentary adults. This association was similar across age groups and genders. Conclusion: Regular running is associated with better sleep quality in population-level data, though causality cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional analysis.

title: Effects of Evening Exercise Timing on Sleep Onset and Nocturnal Awakenings
abstract: Background: Exercise timing may influence sleep, but evidence is mixed. Methods: Twelve healthy adults (mean age 35 years) participated in a within-subjects crossover design. Each participant completed three conditions in random order, separated by 2 weeks: (1) exercise in the morning (7 AM), (2) exercise in the evening (6 PM), or (3) no exercise control. Exercise consisted of 45 minutes of treadmill running at 70% VO2 max. Sleep was measured using polysomnography. Results: Sleep latency was significantly shorter after morning exercise (11.2 min) compared to evening (16.8 min, p=0.03) and control (14.5 min, p=0.07). No significant differences in sleep duration or architecture. Conclusion: Morning exercise may facilitate sleep onset better than evening exercise in some individuals. Larger studies in diverse populations are needed.
